title: CSS layout: cascade, box, flex, grid (variant 1)
description: Predict where boxes land and which rule wins; choose the fix that survives real content.

questions.stem: Both rules match the same link in `<nav id="nav" class="menu">`, and the second comes later in the file. Which colour wins?
questions.code:
#nav a { color: gray; }
.menu a.active { color: crimson; }

options.text: crimson, because it comes later in the stylesheet and later rules always win
options.why: Source order only breaks ties between equal specificity.

options.text: crimson, because it has more selectors (three against two)
options.why: Specificity is compared by column (ids, then classes, then types), not by selector count.

options.text: gray, because one id outweighs any number of classes
options.why: #nav a = (1,0,1); .menu a.active = (0,2,1). The id column decides first.

options.text: Whichever the browser parsed last after cache revalidation
options.why: The cascade is deterministic.

questions.explain: Specificity is a triple (ids, classes/attributes/pseudo-classes, types). Compare left to right; source order only matters when all three are equal. Avoid ids in selectors so you never need to fight them.

questions.stem: A design system ships `@layer base { #app p { color: red; } }`. Your own stylesheet, not in any layer, has `p { color: blue; }`. No `!important` anywhere. What colour are paragraphs?

options.text: red, because #app p is far more specific than a bare p selector
options.why: Layers are compared before specificity.

options.text: blue, because unlayered styles beat layered styles for normal declarations
options.why: In the cascade, layer order is checked before specificity, and unlayered styles count as the last (strongest) layer.

options.text: red, because layers always win over unlayered CSS
options.why: The opposite holds for normal declarations (it flips for !important).

options.text: It depends on which file loads first
options.why: Load order decides layer order, but unlayered still beats any layer.

questions.explain: Cascade layers let you rank whole groups of CSS: `@layer reset, base, components;`. Specificity only competes inside the same layer. That is how you stop specificity wars with third-party CSS.

questions.stem: You write a reusable reset: `:where(ul, ol) { margin: 0; }`. A teammate then writes `ul { margin: 1rem; }` in a component. Which margin applies, and why did you pick `:where`?

options.text: 1rem, because `:where()` has zero specificity, so any later rule overrides the reset easily
options.why: `:where()` always contributes 0; `ul` is (0,0,1), so it wins.

options.text: 0, because `:where()` takes the specificity of its most specific argument
options.why: That describes `:is()`, not `:where()`.

options.text: 0, because the reset is listed first and resets are applied last by the browser
options.why: Browsers have no special 'reset' stage.

options.text: 1rem, but only in Chromium; Safari treats `:where` like `:is` for specificity purposes
options.why: `:where()` is specified and implemented with zero specificity across modern browsers.

questions.explain: `:is()` takes the specificity of its strongest argument; `:where()` always has zero. Use `:where` for defaults you want to be easy to override (resets, library base styles).

questions.stem: A card has `width: 300px; padding: 20px; border: 2px solid;` and no `box-sizing` rule. How wide is it on screen, and what single rule makes it exactly 300px?

options.text: 300px already, because width always includes padding and border
options.why: That's border-box behaviour; the default is content-box.

options.text: 344px; add `box-sizing: border-box`
options.why: content-box: 300 + 2×20 padding + 2×2 border = 344. border-box makes width include padding and border.

options.text: 340px, because borders draw inside the padding area and never add any width to the box
options.why: Borders add width in content-box (2px each side).

options.text: 344px; add `overflow: hidden`
options.why: Overflow clips content; it doesn't change the box size.

questions.explain: Most projects set `*, *::before, *::after { box-sizing: border-box; }` once, so a width means the whole visible box.

questions.stem: Two stacked `<section>`s: the first has `margin-bottom: 24px`, the second `margin-top: 16px`. In normal block flow the gap is A. You then make their parent `display: flex; flex-direction: column;`. The gap becomes B. What are A and B?

options.text: A = 40px, B = 40px
options.why: In block flow, vertical margins between siblings collapse.

options.text: A = 24px, B = 24px, because margins always collapse no matter which layout mode is used
options.why: Flex (and grid) items don't collapse margins.

options.text: A = 24px, B = 40px
options.why: Block flow collapses to the larger margin (24). Flex items' margins don't collapse, so they add (24 + 16).

options.text: A = 16px, B = 24px
options.why: Collapsing keeps the larger margin, not the smaller.

questions.explain: Margin collapsing is a block-flow rule. That's one reason modern layouts use `gap` on a flex or grid parent instead of margins on children: the spacing doesn't change with the layout mode.

questions.stem: A modal has `position: fixed; z-index: 9999` but appears **under** the site header (`z-index: 10`). The modal is rendered inside a `.page` wrapper that has `transform: translateX(0)` for an animation. What is the real fix?

options.text: Raise the modal to `z-index: 999999` so it beats every other element
options.why: The modal's z-index only counts inside the wrapper's stacking context; no number escapes it.

options.text: Render the modal outside `.page` (e.g. a React portal to `document.body`), or remove the transform
options.why: `transform` creates a stacking context (and a containing block for fixed elements). The whole wrapper is ranked against the header.

options.text: Give the header a negative z-index
options.why: It can push the header behind page content and break its own clicks.

options.text: Use `position: absolute` instead
options.why: Still inside the same stacking context.

questions.explain: z-index only competes within a stacking context. `transform`, `filter`, `opacity < 1`, `isolation: isolate`, and positioned elements with a z-index all create one. Overlays go to the top of the document (portal or `<dialog>`'s top layer).

questions.stem: A table of contents has `position: sticky; top: 0;` but scrolls away with the page. Its grandparent `.layout` has `overflow: hidden` (added to hide a horizontal scrollbar). Why doesn't it stick?

options.text: Sticky only works on elements that are inside a CSS grid or flex container
options.why: Sticky works in any layout; grid/flex only change how much room it has.

options.text: `top: 0` should be `top: 0px`, because sticky ignores unitless zero
options.why: Unitless 0 is valid for lengths.

options.text: `overflow: hidden` makes `.layout` the scroll container it sticks to, and that box itself doesn't scroll
options.why: Sticky positions relative to the nearest ancestor with a scrolling mechanism; the page scroll no longer counts.

options.text: Sticky needs a `z-index` to work
options.why: z-index affects painting order, not whether it sticks.

questions.explain: When sticky fails, walk up the ancestors looking for `overflow` other than visible. To hide horizontal overflow without breaking sticky, use `overflow-x: clip` (clip doesn't create a scroll container).

questions.stem: A sidebar needs to fill the full height of its parent row, so you give it `height: 100%`. The parent has no height set and is a normal block. The sidebar stays as short as its content. What works?

options.text: Make the parent `display: flex` (or grid): items stretch to the row height by default
options.why: `align-items: stretch` is the default, so the sidebar matches its tallest sibling without any height.

options.text: Use `height: 100vh`, since that is the same as full parent height
options.why: That's the viewport, not the parent; it overflows or leaves gaps.

options.text: Use `min-height: 100%`, because unlike height it resolves without a definite parent height
options.why: Percent min-height has the same requirement and also resolves to auto.

options.text: Add `!important` to the height rule
options.why: The rule already applies; the percent just has nothing to resolve against.

questions.explain: Percentage heights need a parent with a definite height; otherwise they behave like `auto`. Equal-height columns are what flex and grid stretching are for.

questions.stem: A row is `display: flex`. The middle child holds a long filename with `white-space: nowrap; overflow: hidden; text-overflow: ellipsis;` but instead of an ellipsis the whole row overflows its container. Which one-line fix makes the ellipsis appear?

options.text: Add `flex-shrink: 1` to the middle child so it is allowed to shrink inside the row
options.why: flex-shrink is already 1 by default; the minimum size is what stops it.

options.text: `min-width: 0` on the middle child
options.why: Flex items default to `min-width: auto`, which won't shrink below the text's width. 0 lets it shrink and the ellipsis kicks in.

options.text: `width: 100%` on the middle child
options.why: Makes it want even more space; still can't go below min-content.

options.text: `display: block` on the row
options.why: Loses the flex layout entirely.

questions.explain: The 'flex child won't shrink' bug is almost always `min-width: auto`. Set `min-width: 0` (or `overflow: hidden` on the item) whenever a flex item contains long text, code or a table.

questions.stem: Three tab buttons with labels 'All', 'Archived' and 'Shared with me' should be the **same width** and fill the row. Which item rule does that?

options.text: `flex: auto`, so each tab grows to share the free space evenly
options.why: auto = 1 1 auto: it starts from content width, so longer labels stay wider.

options.text: `flex: 1`
options.why: 1 = 1 1 0%: every item starts from zero and gets an equal share of the space.

options.text: `flex-grow: 1` alone
options.why: Basis stays auto (content width), so widths differ, like flex: auto.

options.text: `justify-content: space-between` on the row
options.why: Spreads the gaps, doesn't size the items.

questions.explain: The basis is the starting size before growing. `flex: 1` (basis 0) = equal widths; `flex: auto` (basis auto) = content-proportional. Equal tabs, equal columns → `flex: 1` (or grid with `1fr` columns).

questions.stem: A login form column is `display: flex; flex-direction: column; justify-content: center;`. The fields are vertically centred but stuck to the left. You want them centred horizontally too. What do you add?

options.text: `justify-content: center` a second time, after the first one in the same rule
options.why: It's already set; in a column it works vertically.

options.text: `align-items: center`
options.why: In a column the cross axis is horizontal, and align-items controls the cross axis.

options.text: `text-align: center`
options.why: Centres inline text inside each box, not the boxes.

options.text: `flex-direction: row` and `justify-content: center`
options.why: Puts the fields side by side.

questions.explain: justify-content = along the main axis (flex-direction); align-items = across it. Switching to `column` swaps which one is horizontal.

questions.stem: A 700px wide grid has `grid-template-columns: repeat(auto-fill, minmax(200px, 1fr))` and no gap. It holds only **two** cards, and they look narrow with an empty column beside them. What changes if you use `auto-fit` instead?

options.text: Nothing; the two keywords are aliases kept for backward compatibility
options.why: They differ exactly when there are fewer items than tracks.

options.text: The empty track collapses and the two cards stretch to 350px each
options.why: Three 200px tracks fit. auto-fill keeps the empty third (cards ~233px); auto-fit collapses it, so the 1fr cards share all 700px.

options.text: The cards drop to exactly 200px wide each and leave a 300px gap on the right side
options.why: minmax(…, 1fr) lets them grow; they never stop at 200px with free space.

options.text: The grid switches to one column
options.why: Track count depends on width (3 fit), not on keyword.

questions.explain: Both create as many tracks as fit. auto-fill keeps empty ones (stable column widths); auto-fit collapses empty ones (items stretch). Card galleries with few items usually want auto-fit.

questions.stem: A two-column layout uses `grid-template-columns: 1fr 1fr`. When a long URL or a wide code block appears in the left column, it becomes much wider than the right one. Which change keeps the columns equal?

options.text: Set the columns to `50% 50%` instead of fractions
options.why: With a gap that overflows, and long content still overflows the track.

options.text: `grid-template-columns: minmax(0, 1fr) minmax(0, 1fr)`
options.why: `1fr` means `minmax(auto, 1fr)`; auto lets min-content push the track wider. A 0 minimum lets it shrink.

options.text: `grid-auto-flow: dense` so the long content is moved to a different track
options.why: Changes placement order, not track sizing.

options.text: `width: 50%` on the left child
options.why: The track itself already grew; the child just follows it.

questions.explain: fr tracks have an automatic minimum (the content's min-content size). For truly equal columns use `minmax(0, 1fr)`, and pair it with `overflow-wrap: anywhere` or a scrolling `pre` for long content.

questions.stem: A heading uses `font-size: clamp(1rem, 2.5vw, 2rem)`. The root font size is the browser default. On a phone 400px wide, how big is the text?

options.text: 10px, because 2.5vw of a 400px wide viewport is exactly 10px
options.why: clamp never goes below its minimum (1rem).

options.text: 16px
options.why: 2.5vw = 10px is below the 1rem (16px) minimum, so clamp returns the minimum.

options.text: 32px
options.why: That's the maximum, used only on wide screens (≥ 1280px here).

options.text: It depends on the parent's font size
options.why: rem uses the root font size; vw uses the viewport. The parent doesn't matter.

questions.explain: `clamp(min, preferred, max)` = fluid type with floors and ceilings. A common recipe mixes units in the middle (`1rem + 1.5vw`) so text still responds to the user's zoom and font settings.

questions.stem: The same `<ProductCard>` sits in a narrow sidebar and in a wide main column. It should stack vertically when **the card's own space** is under 400px, whatever the viewport. A media query can't do that. What is the setup?

options.text: `@container (max-width: 400px)` written inside the card's own CSS, with no other setup needed
options.why: A container query needs a named or typed container ancestor; with none, it never matches.

options.text: Give the card's wrapper `container-type: inline-size`, then style the card inside `@container (width < 400px)`
options.why: The wrapper becomes a query container; the card is styled by the wrapper's width.

options.text: Use a `ResizeObserver` in React to set a class on the card from its measured width
options.why: Works but is the JS workaround that container queries replaced.

options.text: Use `@media (max-width: 400px)` on the sidebar
options.why: Media queries see the viewport, not the sidebar.

questions.explain: Container queries make components responsive to where they are placed. An element can't query itself: set `container-type` on an ancestor (often a wrapper div), then write `@container` rules for the children.
